lessons.title: Keep the buffer warm
lessons.task: Replace out with doubled input values, preserving its existing allocation when capacity is sufficient.
lessons.hint: Clear the vector, then extend it. Do not replace out with a new Vec.
body: Vec stores initialized elements contiguously. Its length tracks valid elements; capacity tracks space available before growth requires reallocation. Never access spare capacity as initialized values.

clear drops existing elements and sets length to zero while retaining the allocation. Reusing a scratch buffer avoids repeatedly requesting storage. It also retains peak capacity, which can waste memory after a large request.
This exercise checks pointer stability only when capacity is already sufficient. It does not assume an allocator growth factor or exact capacity.

lessons.title: A value in the unused space
lessons.task: Map zero to None and every other input to Some(NonZeroU32).
lessons.hint: Use NonZeroU32::new, which validates the value.
body: NonZeroU32 excludes zero from its valid values. Rust guarantees Option<NonZeroU32> has the same size and alignment as NonZeroU32: the unused representation can encode None.

This guarantee applies to documented types, not every enum. Do not assume arbitrary Rust struct field order or transmute values based on a guessed layout. repr(C) serves interoperability; it is not a promise of better performance.
Compact representations can reduce memory traffic in large collections. They also constrain the domain: zero must really be invalid in your identifier model.

lessons.title: Know when resources end
lessons.task: Create and drop one Guard in an inner scope, then return the observed drop count.
lessons.hint: Let the Guard go out of scope before reading the Cell.
body: Rust runs Drop when an owned value leaves scope normally, including ordinary early returns. RAII ties resource release to ownership: a guard can unlock a mutex or return a buffer when dropped.
Cleanup still performs real work. Dropping a large collection may have a visible cost. Moving a value transfers responsibility; cloning can create a second resource whose cleanup also costs time.

An inner scope makes release timing explicit. Destructors are not guaranteed during process abort, and mem::forget can intentionally prevent them, so memory safety must not rely on every destructor running.
